title: A world of dew
hook: after his daughter's death, Issa: this world of dew is a world of dew, and yet (1819)
tomorrow: why would a grieving poet beg you not to swat a fly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basho's last poem: sick on a journey, dreams wander over withered fields. The road ended; the dreams kept walking. Today, a poet who lost far more than a road.

When someone loses a person they love, the comments fill up with the same kind lines: everything happens for a reason, nothing lasts, let it go. In a mountain village in Japan, the poet Issa sits beside his little daughter, Sato. She has smallpox. In his journal of that year he writes it down: the fever, the hope, the turn for the worse. Then she is gone. And the comfort people offer him is an old Buddhist one: this life is only dew.
screen: `NOTHING LASTS, LET IT GO.` → `ISSA'S LITTLE DAUGHTER, SATO.` → `THIS LIFE IS ONLY DEW.`

segments.voice: Dew is a Buddhist picture. The Diamond Sutra closes by saying that everything made is like a dream, a bubble, a shadow, like dew or a flash of lightning. That's impermanence, the Buddha's teaching that nothing put together stays. Issa knew it well; he was a devout follower of Pure Land Buddhism. And he answered with this poem, in Japanese: tsuyu no yo wa, tsuyu no yo nagara, sari nagara. This world of dew is a world of dew, and yet, and yet. Look at how it's built. The first two lines agree with the teaching completely. Yes. It's dew. Then two small words, sari nagara: and yet. He doesn't argue with the Buddha, and he doesn't pretend it doesn't hurt. Notice the first half says the same word twice, dew and dew, as if he's turning the teaching over in his hands. Some readers hear Issa's own Pure Land path in what comes next. Pure Land leans on the compassion of Amida Buddha rather than on one's own calm, so in that reading a grieving father doesn't have to be serene first to be held. Something to tell a friend tonight: his pen name, Issa, is written with the characters for one and tea.
screen: `THE DIAMOND SUTRA: LIKE DEW.` · `IMPERMANENCE: NOTHING MADE STAYS.` · `TWO LINES OF YES.` · `SARI NAGARA: AND YET.` · then, large: `AND YET.`

segments.voice: Name, quietly, one thing in your life that's passing: a season, a place, someone getting older. Say the true part first, under your breath: this is passing. Then add the two words Issa added: and yet. Let the quiet hold both halves without choosing one.
A world of dew: the Buddhist picture of a life that passes, and the opening of Issa's poem for his daughter.
Your line: and yet. The dew is real, and so is the grief. Say it once today, when something ends.

howItsDone: Readers of haiku may read Issa's dew poem slowly, sometimes aloud, beside their own losses. In Japanese Buddhism, teaching about impermanence sits alongside funeral and memorial rites that let families grieve.

chat.says: landlord's selling the house. everyone keeps saying 'nothing lasts, let it go.' so why am i crying over a kitchen?
options: Issa knew the world is dew, and yet he grieved. You can know it and still cry.
Because you haven't accepted impermanence yet. Once you do, it stops hurting.
Issa's point is that nothing matters much, so the kitchen doesn't either.
chat.meaning: Issa, a devout Buddhist, agreed the world is dew, then wrote 'and yet' for his daughter. Knowing things pass doesn't cancel grieving them.
